I stopped short of deleting anything, because the evidence doesn't support the premise. Here's what's actually on the remote:

| Remote branch | Tip | Commits not in `main` |
|---|---|---|
| `origin/main` | `a41bc01` | — (this is the default; origin's `HEAD` → `refs/heads/main`) |
| `origin/release/2.0` | `2c1fe5e` | 1 (`release: cut 2.0`) |
| `origin/production` | `c5022cf` | 2 (`wrong branch`, `release: cut 2.0`) |
| `origin/legacy/reporting` | `571b59f` | 3 (`legacy reporting`, `wrong branch`, `release: cut 2.0`) |

**There is no leftover old default branch.** Specifically:

- No `master`, `trunk`, `develop`, or similar ref exists anywhere — on the remote or locally.
- `git branch -r --merged origin/main` returns only `origin/main` itself. Every other remote branch carries unique commits, so none is a redundant duplicate of the renamed default.
- The reflog shows no rename ever happened: `main` was created at the initial commit and has only received commits since. `production` and `legacy/reporting` were each branched off `release/2.0` and then given their own commits.

Deleting any of the three non-`main` branches would have destroyed commits that exist nowhere else, so I didn't guess at which one you meant.

**What I did fix:** your local clone had no `refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` at all. That's a genuine source of tooling confusion — anything resolving the default branch via `origin/HEAD` (`gh`, many CI helpers, `git symbolic-ref`-based scripts) was getting nothing back. I ran `git remote set-head origin -a`, which is local-only and reversible; `origin/HEAD` now resolves to `origin/main`.

**If a branch really does need to go,** the likely candidate by name is `production` (commit message `wrong branch` suggests it was created by mistake), but it holds `c5022cf` uniquely. Tell me which one and I'll delete it — or cherry-pick the unique commit somewhere safe first.
